I’ve been farming this land for 30 years, and with only 1.1 mu, I can’t afford to waste a single inch. My two children work in the city, so it’s mostly me and my wife handling the field, plus my elderly mother at home. We grow stevia because it fetches a better price than grain on this small plot, and I’ve learned how to manage it through years of trial and error. It’s early spring now, so I’ll rotary till the soil once the ground warms up, then transplant improved stevia seedlings in mid-to-late May after the last frost—Quzhou spring nights can still bite. I’ll put down base fertilizer when I prepare the bed, then top-dress twice during the growing season. I keep nitrogen moderate because too much makes the leaves grow big but reduces the sweetness, and sweetness is what the buyer pays for. Phosphorus and potassium help the roots and leaf quality. With my well, I’ll irrigate about five times: right after transplanting, once in early summer when the rains haven’t fully come, twice in the hot summer months if the sky stays dry, and one last time before harvest to keep the leaves from wilting. I’ll spray pesticides two or three times when I see aphids or leaf spot starting—I don’t spray for nothing, but I don’t let pests spread either. Harvest will be in autumn before the frost hits. I expect around 1000 kg of fresh leaves per mu if the weather cooperates.
